hints: Look at Fig. 6.2 with V on one axis and Q on the other. Think about building up charge on a capacitor little by little and what multiplying a small p.d. by a small charge tells you.
Read the charge $Q$ when $V = 8.0\text{ V}$ from the straight line, convert $\mu\text{C}$ to $\text{C}$, then find the area of the triangle under the line.
walkthrough:
**Why area means energy**
Think of charging in tiny steps. Moving a tiny charge $\Delta Q$ across a p.d. $V$ needs work $V \Delta Q$. Adding up all those little rectangles gives the total work, which is the area under the $V$ against $Q$ graph. Because the line starts at the origin, the shape is a triangle.

**Read the starting values and calculate**
At $t=0$ the capacitor is fully charged to $$V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$$ From Fig. 6.2 the corresponding charge is $$Q_0 = 450\,\mu\text{C} = 450 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}$$ Area of triangle: $$E = \frac{1}{2} \times Q_0 \times V_0$$ $$E = \frac{1}{2} \times 450 \times 10^{-6} \times 8.0 = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J}$$ That is $1.8\text{ mJ}$, as required.

Final answer: At $t=0$, $V = 8.0\text{ V}$ and $Q = 450\,\mu\text{C}$. $E = \text{area} = \frac{1}{2}QV = \frac{1}{2} \times 450 \times 10^{-6} \times 8.0 = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ J} = 1.8\text{ mJ}$.

hints: You now know the charge on the plates and the p.d. across them at $t=0$. Recall how capacitance links charge stored to p.d. applied.
Use $Q = 450\,\mu\text{C}$ and $V = 8.0\text{ V}$ with consistent SI units to get $C$ in farads.
walkthrough:
**Link Q, V and C**
Capacitance tells you how much charge is stored per volt: $$C = \frac{Q}{V}$$ You can read $Q$ and $V$ straight from Fig. 6.2. Equivalently the gradient of the $V$-$Q$ line is $1/C$.

**Put numbers in**
$$Q_0 = 450 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C}, \quad V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$$ $$C = \frac{450 \times 10^{-6}}{8.0} = 5.6 \times 10^{-5}\text{ F}$$ So about $56\,\mu\text{F}$. The unit is the farad, $\text{F}$.

hints: Start from how p.d. falls during discharge through a resistor. Remember the exponential law involves $V_0$, $t$, $R$ and $C$, and that $RC$ has a special name.
Set $t$ equal to that $RC$ combination and take natural logs of both sides to isolate $-\ln(V/V_0)$. Recall $V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$ here.
walkthrough:
**Write the discharge equation**
For discharge through resistor $R$: $$V = V_0 e^{-t/RC}$$ Here the starting p.d. is $$V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$$ The product $RC$ controls how fast the decay is and is called the time constant: $$\tau = RC$$ So you can write more simply: $$V = V_0 e^{-t/\tau}$$

**Put t = tau and take logs**
When $t = \tau$: $$\frac{V}{V_0} = e^{-\tau/\tau} = e^{-1}$$ With $V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$: $$\frac{V}{8.0} = e^{-1}$$ Take natural log: $$\ln\left(\frac{V}{8.0}\right) = -1$$ Multiply by $-1$: $$-\ln\left(\frac{V}{8.0}\right) = 1.0$$ That is exactly what Fig. 6.3 plots on its vertical axis.
Final answer: $V = V_0 e^{-t/RC}$ with $V_0 = 8.0\text{ V}$ and $\tau = RC$. At $t = \tau$, $V/8.0 = e^{-1}$, so $\ln(V/8.0) = -1$ and $-\ln(V/8.0) = 1.0$.

hints: From the last result, one time constant corresponds to a vertical-axis value of 1.0 on Fig. 6.3. Find 1.0 on that axis and read across to the line then down to $t$.
walkthrough:
**Read tau from the straight line**
You have shown $t = \tau$ gives $-\ln(V/8.0) = 1.0$. On Fig. 6.3 go up to $1.0$ on the vertical axis, across to the line, then down to the $t$-axis. This gives: $$\tau \approx 3.2\text{ s}$$
Final answer: $\tau = 3.2\text{ s}$ read from Fig. 6.3 at $-\ln(V/8.0) = 1.0$.

hints: You now have $\tau$ from the discharge graph and $C$ from part (a). Recall how $\tau$, $R$ and $C$ are linked for a capacitor-resistor circuit.
Rearrange to make $R$ the subject and substitute $\tau \approx 3.2\text{ s}$ and $C \approx 5.6 \times 10^{-5}\text{ F}$.
walkthrough:
**Use tau = RC**
The time constant combines both components: $$\tau = RC$$ So resistance is: $$R = \frac{\tau}{C}$$ A larger $R$ or larger $C$ makes discharge slower, which makes sense.
